facts.title: Named For Mendeleev
facts.text: Mendelevium honors Dmitri Mendeleev, the Russian chemist who published the first widely recognized periodic table in 1869. The name was a deliberate Cold War gesture: in 1955 American scientists chose to celebrate a Russian whose table had famously predicted undiscovered elements. It was the first element named after a person who created the periodic system itself.

facts.title: Discovered One Atom At A Time
facts.text: In 1955 a Berkeley team led by Albert Ghiorso, Glenn Seaborg, Bernard Harvey, Gregory Choppin and Stanley Thompson made mendelevium by bombarding einsteinium-253 with alpha particles in the 60-inch cyclotron. The experiment produced only about one atom of element 101 per bombardment, and the entire discovery rested on a total of just 17 atoms. It was the first element ever discovered by detecting single atoms, one event at a time.

facts.title: A Clever Chemistry Trick
facts.text: Because so few atoms existed, the team could not weigh or see mendelevium, so they identified it chemically using ion-exchange columns. They predicted that Md atoms would wash off the column in a specific order relative to other actinides and then watched for the telltale radioactive decay in exactly the predicted drops. This elegant elution method let them prove a brand-new element from a handful of invisible atoms.

facts.title: It Breaks The Actinide Rule
facts.text: Most actinides strongly prefer the +3 oxidation state in water, but mendelevium also forms a surprisingly stable +2 ion. This unusual stability comes from its nearly filled 5f electron shell, which makes the divalent state energetically favorable. Studying Md helped chemists understand how the actinide series differs from the lighter rare-earth elements above it.

facts.title: A Half-Life Of Weeks
facts.text: The longest-lived isotope, mendelevium-258, has a half-life of about 51.5 days, far longer than most isotopes of its neighbors. This relative stability makes it the workhorse isotope for laboratory chemistry experiments on the element. Even so, a sample would noticeably weaken within a couple of months as it radioactively decays.

facts.title: Vanishingly Rare On Earth
facts.text: Mendelevium does not occur naturally anywhere on Earth and must be created atom by atom in particle accelerators or reactors. Scientists have never assembled a weighable, visible quantity of the metal, so its bulk appearance and melting point are estimated rather than measured. Everything humans have ever made of it would be invisible to the naked eye.

facts.title: Born From Other Synthetic Elements
facts.text: To make mendelevium, researchers first had to manufacture its target, einsteinium, which itself does not exist in nature. Einsteinium-253 was so precious that only a few billion atoms could be prepared, then coated onto a thin gold foil for bombardment. This made Md a synthetic element built from another synthetic element, a chain of human-made matter.

facts.title: Purely For Pure Science
facts.text: Mendelevium has no commercial, industrial, or medical applications, and given its scarcity and rapid decay it likely never will. Its only real-world value is scientific: testing predictions about electron structure, oxidation states, and the limits of the periodic table. It is a classic example of research pursued to understand nature rather than to build a product.

facts.title: Self-Heating And Self-Destructive
facts.text: Like other heavy actinides, mendelevium is intensely radioactive, and its decay releases enough energy that a macroscopic lump would heat itself and damage its own crystal structure. The emitted radiation steadily breaks chemical bonds and disrupts any container holding it. This self-destruction is one reason no large sample has ever been kept intact.

facts.title: A Window Into Relativity
facts.text: In very heavy atoms like mendelevium, inner electrons move at a large fraction of the speed of light, so Einstein's relativity measurably changes their energy levels. These relativistic effects help explain why Md favors its unusual +2 state and behaves differently from lighter elements with similar configurations. Element 101 thus serves as a real laboratory for testing how relativity reshapes chemistry.
